content: Sweating sickness, also referred to as the English sweat (Latin: sudor anglicus), was a mysterious and highly lethal disease that struck England and parts of Europe in a series of epidemics between 1485 and 1551, after which it seemingly disappeared. The disease was characterized by an abrupt and dramatic onset of symptoms, often leading to death within hours. Its exact cause remains unknown. It is important to note that sweating sickness is unrelated to hyperhidrosis, a condition also informally referred to as sweating disease. The first recorded outbreak of sweating sickness occurred in 1485, coinciding with the early reign of Henry VII. Reports of the disease emerged shortly after Henry's landing at Milford Haven on August 7, 1485, and before the Battle of Bosworth Field on August 22. By the time Henry entered London on August 28, the disease had already begun to spread in the capital, killing thousands by late October. Among the victims were two lord mayors, six aldermen, and three sheriffs. The disease was distinct from other known epidemics of the time, such as the plague or pestilential fever, due to its unique symptoms and rapid fatality. After the initial outbreak in 1485, the disease re-emerged in 1507, though this second epidemic was less severe. A third outbreak occurred in 1517 and was significantly more devastating, with reports of high mortality in towns such as Oxford and Cambridge, where up to half the population may have perished. This outbreak also spread to Calais and Antwerp but remained largely confined to England. The fourth epidemic in 1528 was particularly severe and marked the first time the disease spread beyond England. It began in London in late May and quickly spread across the country, though it did not reach the far north of England, Scotland, or Ireland. The mortality rate in London was high, prompting King Henry VIII to leave the city and frequently change his residence. Anne Boleyn is believed to have contracted and survived the illness during this time. The disease then spread to mainland Europe, appearing suddenly in Hamburg and causing over a thousand deaths within weeks. It continued to spread rapidly, reaching Switzerland, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Lithuania, Poland, and Russia. However, it never appeared in France or Italy. In Belgium and the Netherlands, the disease emerged simultaneously in Antwerp and Amsterdam on September 27, likely transmitted directly from England. In each affected location, the disease typically lasted no more than two weeks before disappearing. By the end of 1528, it had vanished from most of Europe, except for eastern Switzerland, where it lingered into the following year. After this outbreak, sweating sickness did not reappear on the European mainland. In Ireland, the disease was recorded in 1492, with the Annals of Ulster documenting the death of James Fleming, Baron of Slane, from the pláigh allais (sweating plague). The Annals of Connacht and the Annals of the Four Masters also mention an unusual plague in Meath that lasted only 24 hours, with survivors recovering fully after this period. However, some historians, such as Freeman, have argued that this illness may have been a different disease, such as relapsing fever or famine fever, rather than sweating sickness. The final major outbreak of sweating sickness occurred in England in 1551. John Caius, a prominent physician of the time, provided a detailed eyewitness account of the disease in his work A Boke or Counseill Against the Disease Commonly Called the Sweate, or Sweatyng Sicknesse. The symptoms of sweating sickness, as described by Caius and other contemporaries, began suddenly with a sense of apprehension, followed by cold shivers (sometimes severe), dizziness, headache, and intense pain in the neck, shoulders, and limbs, accompanied by profound exhaustion. This initial cold stage lasted between 30 minutes and three hours and was followed by a hot stage characterized by profuse sweating, a sensation of heat, headache, delirium, rapid pulse, and extreme thirst. Palpitations and chest pain were also common. Unlike other febrile illnesses, no skin eruptions were observed. In the final stages, patients often experienced either collapse from exhaustion or an overwhelming urge to sleep, which was considered fatal if indulged. Notably, surviving one episode of the disease did not confer immunity, and some individuals suffered multiple attacks before succumbing. After 1578, the disease was never seen again in England. However, a similar illness known as the Picardy sweat appeared in France between 1718 and 1861. This illness was less fatal and was accompanied by a rash, which was not a feature of the original sweating sickness. The cause of sweating sickness remains one of its most enigmatic aspects. Contemporary and modern commentators have speculated that the unsanitary conditions of the time, including poor hygiene and sewage management, may have played a role in harboring the source of infection. The first outbreak's timing, at the end of the Wars of the Roses, has led to theories that the disease may have been introduced to England by French mercenaries who fought for Henry VII, as they appeared to be immune. Interestingly, the disease seemed to affect the wealthy more severely than the poor, which may explain why it was considered noteworthy compared to other illnesses of the era. Several hypotheses have been proposed regarding the etiology of sweating sickness. Relapsing fever, a disease transmitted by ticks and lice and more common in summer months, has been suggested. However, relapsing fever is typically associated with a black scab at the site of the tick bite and a subsequent rash, neither of which were noted in historical accounts of sweating sickness. More recently, Hantavirus has been proposed as a potential cause. While Hantavirus shares some clinical similarities with sweating sickness, such as rapid onset and high mortality, it is rarely transmitted from person to person, whereas human-to-human transmission was believed to be significant in sweating sickness. These discrepancies leave the true cause of the disease unresolved, and other theories remain under consideration.
